title: Partial Lasserre relaxation for sparse Max-Cut
contribution: Strengthens the sparse first-level Lasserre relaxation of Max-Cut with level-2 PSD constraints on chordal-extension cliques of size at most r (partial) and on selected r-subsets of larger cliques (augmented, five selection heuristics), and shows that it beats BiqCrunch and CS-TSSOS on sparse graphs with small cliques and loses as cliques grow.
problem_entry: Level 2 of even the sparse Lasserre hierarchy is unsolvable beyond about 30 nodes (the authors' own failed 300-node runs), while level 1 is weak; the entry point is the space between the two levels (pp. 2, 5-6).
key_idea: Lift to level 2 only the cliques of the chordal extension with at most r nodes (Relaxation 6), optionally adding p heuristic r-subsets of larger cliques (Relaxation 7, heuristics H1-H5); cliques are chosen by graph pattern rather than by learned scores (pp. 3, 6-7).
assumptions: Max-Cut as a +-1 POP with Laplacian objective; the sparse hierarchy depends only on graph sparsity; convergence results for the running-intersection property cited (Lasserre 2006); random instances from SparsePOP randomUnconst.m (pp. 2, 4-6, 8).
proof_devices: Containment by citation: dense level 2 inside the metric polytope, Anjos-Wolkowicz proof transferred to Lasserre in a footnote (pp. 10-11)
For r <= 4, MET1st+ at least as tight as Relaxation (6) because metric-polytope vertices are cuts on 3-4 nodes (p. 12)
Numerical counterexample: an explicit point on a 5-clique in MET1st+ for which the level-2 PSD feasibility problem has no solution, so the sets differ for r >= 5 (footnote 2, p. 12)
experiments: 240 random graphs (n = 300/500, u = 4-10, three weight sets), Biq Mac toroidal Ising grids, ten CS-TSSOS instances up to 5005 nodes; BiqCrunch time-to-match with the fastest of 4 (or 8) settings kept; time tables with and without the authors' clique construction; CS-TSSOS total vs IPM time; heuristic ranking with a random control; reference values not all certified; losses for dense graphs printed (pp. 8-20).
positioning: Claims to be the first computational study of sparse intermediate Lasserre levels; credits Josz-Molzahn's multi-order relaxation as the same idea and reports that Chen et al. 2022 later generalised it; concedes that linear branch-and-cut beats Biq Mac on toroidal grids (pp. 2-3).
writing: Short and table-driven (11 tables); claims scoped to sparse graphs with small cliques every time; specific hedging ('there is not a clear pattern'); own prototype code called improvable (pp. 3, 14-15, 20).
limits_future: Loses power as density or clique size grows; how to choose r and p is left open, with multilevel techniques suggested (pp. 20-21).

method_links.note: Family between Lasserre levels 1 and 2 indexed by r (and p); random control H1; parameter choice printed as open.
Four BiqCrunch settings, fastest kept (the T3 oracle practice); timings with and without own construction code; uncertified reference values flagged; losses by density printed.
The relaxation is not embedded in a B&B; the full exact solver (BiqCrunch) is the yardstick through time-to-match, not the host.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Explicit point in MET1st+ printed, with a numerically infeasible level-2 PSD feasibility problem, to show that two relaxations are not ordered.

transferable: Show on your own hardware that the next hierarchy level fails at target size before proposing an intermediate relaxation (p. 6).
Give the specialised competitor several parameter settings and keep its best time per instance (p. 11).
Report time tables with and without your prototype preprocessing code (Tables 6-7, pp. 13-15).
Include a random selection rule as a control for selection heuristics and report its rank frequencies (Table 5, p. 14).
Time-to-match: measure how long the exact solver needs to reach your bound, using integrality to define 'as good as' (pp. 11, 15).
Report the structure statistic that drives tractability (clique sizes of the chordal extension) for every instance family (Tables 1, 8, 10).

quotes.text: For each Max-Cut instance, our comparisons are with respect to the fastest time of these four implementations that reached the solution
Although the partial relaxation showed potential, there is still the question of how to select the parameters r and p in the partial relaxation.

title: Augmenting optimization-based molecular design with graph neural networks
contribution: Journal extension (read as arXiv v1) of the GNN-over-molecules MIP: a tighter big-M GNN encoding implemented in OMLT with a PyG interface, a fragment-based CAMD formulation with graph-isomorphism symmetry breaking and chemistry constraints, and odorant case studies solved to optimality up to 12 fragments and to feasibility up to about 25-40.
problem_entry: GNN-based molecular design mostly evaluates the GNN inside GAs or BO instead of solving the inverse problem; the conference version stopped at N = 8 atoms and had no aromaticity (arXiv pp. 2, 17).
key_idea: Encode each GNN layer with a variable adjacency through z = A x big-M constraints (tighter bounds than the conference version), wrap it as an OMLT GNNLayer, and replace atoms by fragments so that structural and symmetry-breaking constraints carry over (arXiv pp. 5-10, 15-17).
assumptions: Fixed weights; linear sum/mean aggregation; GCNConv and mean aggregation unsupported with a non-fixed graph; nonlinear activations inadvisable; interval-arithmetic bounds; exactly N fragments in the experiments (arXiv pp. 4-5, 9-11).
proof_devices: Feasible indexing under (S1)+(S3) for any graph with a chosen node 0, cited from Zhang et al. 2023 and illustrated by its indexing algorithm (arXiv pp. 15-16)
Universal-ordering-vector bijection (powers of 2) for the feature hierarchy (S2) and the neighbour ordering (C27) (arXiv p. 16)
Reordering the symmetry-breaking coefficients so that an existential chemistry requirement becomes a bound on node 0 (B1-B2) (arXiv pp. 18-20)
experiments: Sharma et al. odour data, banana (300 molecules) and garlic (262); 10 GNNs per odour; 5 Gurobi seeds x 10 models = 50 runs per N = 4-12, 10 h limit, quartiles and success counts (9/50 and 5/50 at N = 12); feasibility mode with MIPFocus=1 for N = 15-50, mostly negative objectives at N = 30-40 and 1/20 feasible beyond 40; no competing method (arXiv pp. 22-25).
positioning: Credits McDonald et al. as first and generalises their big-M from GraphSAGE to all linear-aggregation GNNs; inherits the CAMD MIP literature; places itself in the optimisation-over-trained-models line, including her tree and ReLU work (arXiv pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: Four contribution bullets over the conference paper; worked conversion examples for each layer type; each chemistry requirement stated, justified and then linearised; candid that requirements came from inspecting outputs (arXiv pp. 3, 7-8, 20-21).
limits_future: Optimality only up to 12 fragments; the large-N failure is explained only as 'possible'; unsupported layers listed; no explicit future work; modest banana test accuracy (0.703) and no chemist evaluation of designs (not discussed by the paper) (arXiv pp. 10, 23, 25-27).

method_links.note: Trained GNN written as constraints, solved exactly, generalised into OMLT behind a PyG interface; BASF coauthors; public data set.
'Keep near the data' realised as data-set bounds on atom, bond and ring counts (C22-C25) and negative-class filtering, not a PCA penalty.
Graph-isomorphism symmetry (N! indexings) identified as structure and removed by constraints that keep a feasible indexing.
Careful run statistics (50 runs, quartiles, success counts) but no competitor; scaling study only.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Chemistry requirements (no heteroatom chains, S only bonded to C, no allenes, no O-O, at most 2 aromatic rings) added after inspecting the optimiser's molecules, each with a stated chemical reason.

transferable: Open a journal extension by listing the conference version's limits and mapping each new section to one (arXiv pp. 3, 17).
Change the unit of the decision graph (atoms to fragments) so that all structural and symmetry constraints carry over unchanged (arXiv p. 17).
Encode 'there exists a node with property P' by giving P top weight in the symmetry-breaking order, forcing it to index 0 (arXiv pp. 18-20).
Run each size with several trained models and solver seeds; report quartiles and success counts (Tables 6-7, arXiv p. 24).
When optimality stops scaling, switch to a declared feasibility protocol and report where even feasibility fails (arXiv pp. 23, 25).
Publish a supported/unsupported operation table for fixed and variable graph structure alongside worked layer conversions (arXiv pp. 7-10).
coauthors: Shiqiang Zhang, Juan S. Campos, Christian Feldmann, Frederik Sandfort, Miriam Mathea (BASF SE)

quotes.text: These symmetric solutions significantly enlarge the search space and slow down the solving process.
This requirement is included as the optimization results showed a tendency to include a huge amount of connected heteroatoms in suggested structures.

title: Verifying message-passing neural networks via topology-based bounds tightening
contribution: Certifies robustness of ReLU message-passing GNNs against edge additions and removals under local and global budgets by MIP, with static and aggressive (in-tree, local-cut) topology-based bounds tightening in SCIP that makes SCIP about 3x faster and closes much of its gap to Gurobi.
problem_entry: GNN certificates in the literature are restricted to one perturbation type or to GCNs; a MIP encoding admits adding and removing edges, global and local budgets, and feature changes, but is too large for convex-hull ReLU formulations, so the lever is the big-M bounds (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Compute pre-activation bounds from the original neighbours plus the k most negative budget-feasible changes (sbt, closed form by sorting), and recompute them in each B&B node on the graph modified by fixed adjacency variables with the remaining budget (abt), added as local cutting planes (pp. 4-7).
assumptions: ReLU GraphSAGE-type MPNN with fixed weights; P1 (symmetric add/remove, global and local budgets) for graph classification, P2 (removal only, 2-hop neighbourhood) for node classification; only adjacency perturbations tested (pp. 3-4, 8).
proof_devices: Property 3.2: split the neighbour sum into original, added, removed and inactive nodes, so the lower bound is sum of lb plus the best <= qv changes (Eqs. 17-19, pp. 5, 13)
Property 3.4 by reduction to Property 3.2 on the modified graph with reduced budget (Remark 3.5, pp. 6, 13)
Node-local validity handled by local cutting planes valid only in the subtree (pp. 7, 13-14)
Argument that FastLin/CROWN/DeepPoly fail because a binary adjacency breaks inter-layer linearity; OBBT is the only existing method that transfers (p. 6)
experiments: SCIP 8.0.4 single-thread on a shared cluster; ENZYMES, MUTAG (graph), Cora, CiteSeer (node); s in {2,3,4}, global budget 1-10% of edges; SCIPbasic/sbt/abt and GRBbasic/sbt; avg time, shifted geometric mean, number solved, on all and on robust instances; consensus ground truth, inconsistent instances excluded; Gurobi bug reported, buggy version kept with an RHS shift; OBBT control on 44 robust MUTAG instances; sbt about 3x faster than basic, abt not better on average (pp. 6-9, 13-14).
positioning: Divides prior work into attacks and certificates; builds on the group's GNN encoding and Anderson et al.'s ReLU big-M; adopts aggressive bounds tightening from Belotti et al. 2016; notes PySCIPOpt-ML as an alternative host; cites Badilla et al. for tighter-bounds-can-slow results (pp. 1-6, 9).
writing: Three numbered key outcomes in the introduction; a toy figure showing all three bounding schemes on one node; negative results kept; a sbt/abt label swap on p. 6; the 'factor of 10 to 3' claim is not derived in the text (pp. 2, 6, 9).
limits_future: abt does not dominate sbt; node classification too easy to discriminate; feature perturbations untested; no future directions; recommends running sbt and abt in parallel instead of choosing a default (pp. 4, 7, 9).

method_links.note: Graph topology and perturbation budgets used as structure that interval arithmetic ignores; 3x speed-up.
Verification as a MIP over the trained MPNN reusing the group's GNN encoding; the OMLT GNN pull request used to debug the SCIP code.
Judged inside full SCIP/Gurobi B&B and split by answer type, but no default chosen: sbt and abt recommended in parallel.

Consensus ground truth, inconsistent instances excluded, solver bug found and reported, three metrics on two subsets, OBBT control; lapse: buggy Gurobi version kept for lack of time and its infeasible answers dropped rather than counted as failures.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An instance is labelled robust only if every method says so except time-outs; inconsistent instances are excluded.
Neither sbt nor abt dominates, so running both in parallel is recommended, citing MIP portfolio practice.

transferable: When the strongest formulation is too large, tighten big-M coefficients and say why the hull formulation was not used (p. 2).
Derive a closed form ('take the k most negative changes') for budgeted bounds so tightening can run in every B&B node (pp. 5, 13).
Prove the in-tree bound by reduction to the root bound on a modified instance with reduced budget (p. 13).
Label instances only where all solvers agree when ground truth is unknowable; drop inconsistent ones (pp. 9, 13).
Split results by answer type (robust vs non-robust); tightening helps proofs and can hurt counterexample search (pp. 7, 9).
Use OBBT as a tightest-affordable-bounds control and report its cost and per-layer relative bound tightness (p. 14).
Implement branching-dependent bounds as local cuts in a separator callback (pp. 7, 13-14).
Stop the MIP once the sign question is answered instead of solving to optimality (p. 7).
coauthors: Christopher Hojny (TU Eindhoven), Shiqiang Zhang, Juan S. Campos

quotes.text: We cannot know the ground truth of a robust instance without complete enumeration or relying on a solver’s numerical tolerances
we found and reported a small bug in Gurobi wherein several instances were declared infeasible despite having a feasible solution found by SCIP.
